prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- Today is described as a calm day in Beirut, with normal traffic and no dead visible in the streets.
- The city still carries the memory of yesterday’s dead, who are linked to dreams, love, comradeship, resistance, and survival.
- Everyday life continues in the streets, where pedestrians disrupt buses and ignore newspapers that have already moved on.
- The dead are imagined as resting on the Pavement of Martyrs near Sabra, showing that grief remains present beneath the calm.
- A neighbor’s simple “Good morning” becomes a fragile reason to keep living and return to the streets.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem portrays a deceptively calm day in Beirut amid recurring death and political violence, using surreal, elegiac street imagery to contrast ordinary routines with the procession of martyrs. It finds that even peace is haunted by the dead, making daily life inseparable from grief, resistance, and the fragile insistence on staying alive.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Some, Today, Beirut

outputs.L1:
No dead in the streets today: it is a calm day. Traffic is normal; there is ample room for the procession of yesterday’s dead, room to add a dream, an idea, a little boy, an extra push for the beloved boat, a nom de guerre for the cell, a rose for a new love, a hand offered to a comrade. Some room to stay alive for a while—enough time to shake your hands and reach the sun.

Today is a calm day, a pedestrian day in Beirut: people dancing in the streets, obstructing buses, and not buying newspapers. The newspapers have already gone out to the offices, and the dead are resting on the Pavement of Martyrs at the outskirts of Sabra.

A calm day. Our neighbor will step out in her nightgown to hang some sleepiness around us, some sluggish waking; she is too lethargic to gather letters into words.

Where is life on this vast, sauntering morning?

We will not leave.

Out of the whiteness of her gown, a reason will come to carry us down to the streets, dead in her “Good morning.”
outputs.L2:
With no bodies in the streets, today feels quiet. Traffic moves as usual, and there is enough space for the funeral march of those who died yesterday—space too for a dream, for a thought, for a small boy, for one more shove to the cherished boat, for a fighter’s assumed name in the cell, for a rose offered to a new love, for a comrade’s hand. There is still a little room to remain alive awhile, long enough to clasp your hands and stretch toward the sun.

Today is peaceful, an ordinary day for pedestrians in Beirut, where people dance in the roads, hold up the buses, and do not buy newspapers, because the papers have already gone off to the offices and the dead lie resting on the Martyrs’ pavement near Sabra.

It is a quiet day. Our neighbor will come outside in her nightdress and spread a little drowsiness around us, a slow and heavy waking; she is too tired even to assemble letters into words.

Where is life on this broad morning that wanders so slowly? We will not go away. From the white of her gown, some reason will appear and lead us back down into the streets, dead inside her “Good morning.”
outputs.L3:
Today is described as a calm day in Beirut. The streets appear ordinary again: traffic moves as usual, buses follow their routes, and no bodies are visible on the roads. At first glance, the city seems to have returned to its daily rhythm, as if nothing terrible had happened.

Yet beneath this surface calm, Beirut still carries the memory of yesterday’s dead. They remain present in the minds of the living, connected to dreams that were not fulfilled, to love that was interrupted, to comradeship, resistance, and the struggle to survive. Their absence is not empty; it is filled with everything they represented and everything they left behind.

Meanwhile, everyday life continues in the streets. Pedestrians cross carelessly and disrupt the movement of buses. People move through the city with familiar impatience, while newspapers have already shifted their attention elsewhere. The news has moved on, but grief has not. The public world behaves as though the dead belong to yesterday, while those who remember them know they are still part of today.

The dead are imagined as resting on the Pavement of Martyrs near Sabra. This image suggests that mourning lies just beneath the city’s ordinary movements. Even when the streets look calm, they are marked by loss. The martyrs remain close to the living, not hidden away in the past but present in the places people continue to walk through.

In this fragile atmosphere, a neighbor’s simple “Good morning” becomes deeply meaningful. It is a small gesture, but it offers a reason to continue. The greeting reminds the speaker that life, however wounded, still reaches out through ordinary human contact. Because of this brief moment of recognition, it becomes possible to keep living, to step outside again, and to return to the streets of Beirut.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents Beirut as a city suspended between ordinary life and recurring catastrophe. At first, the day appears calm, almost deceptively peaceful: the streets continue to exist, people move through their routines, and the city seems to carry on as if life were simply proceeding. Yet this calm is never innocent. Beneath it lies the constant presence of death, political violence, and collective mourning. The poem’s images turn the familiar urban landscape into something surreal and elegiac, where everyday scenes are shadowed by the procession of martyrs and by the memory of those who have been killed.

Through this contrast, the poem suggests that in Beirut the ordinary and the tragic cannot be separated. A street is not only a street; it is also a place marked by absence, protest, burial, and remembrance. Daily gestures—walking, waiting, watching, surviving—take on a deeper significance because they occur in a city repeatedly wounded by history. The dead do not disappear from public life. They remain present in the imagination of the living, haunting even moments that might otherwise seem peaceful.

The poem therefore refuses to treat peace as simple relief or safety. Instead, peace itself is shown as fragile, haunted, and incomplete. It exists alongside grief and is shaped by the knowledge that violence may return at any moment. The living continue, but their continuation is not passive; it becomes a form of resistance. To remain in the city, to move through its streets, and to insist on ordinary life amid mourning is also to defy the forces that seek to destroy that life.

Ultimately, the poem portrays Beirut as a place where survival is inseparable from memory. Its atmosphere is both tender and unsettling, filled with sorrow but also with endurance. The city’s people live with the dead beside them, carrying grief as part of their daily existence. In doing so, they reveal the fragile but persistent human will to remain alive, to remember, and to resist erasure.
outputs.L5:
Today, Beirut stands as a city of history, resilience, and unforgettable character. Some people know it for its beautiful coastline and lively streets, while others remember its rich culture, music, food, and architecture. The city blends the old and the new, with ancient landmarks standing beside modern cafés, galleries, and neighborhoods full of energy.

Some visitors come to Beirut to enjoy the Mediterranean Sea, while others explore its markets, museums, and vibrant nightlife. Today, despite the challenges it has faced, Beirut continues to inspire many with its strength and spirit. It is a place where stories are shared, traditions are preserved, and hope remains alive in everyday life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about a calm morning in wartime Beirut, with references to Sabra, martyrs, newspapers, neighbors, and the strange coexistence of ordinary life and death.
counterfactuals.output:
At morning, Beirut opens one eye and pretends it has slept.

The sea is pale and careful, folding light over itself like a sheet over a body. In the alleys, the grocer lifts his shutters with the tenderness of a man waking a child. Bread arrives warm, and the newspapers arrive warmer, black with yesterday’s smoke, damp from the hands that pass them along. Men read the names aloud, then lower their voices, as if the martyrs might be resting in the next room.

In Sabra, a woman rinses mint in a blue plastic bowl. The water runs green between her fingers. A radio mutters from a windowsill; somewhere, a rooster insists on the old agreements between dawn and the world. Neighbors call to one another across balconies strung with laundry—shirts, towels, a small dress bright as a flag no army has claimed. They ask after sugar, after children, after a cousin who did not come home. The answers drift upward and hang there with the wet clothes.

How calm the morning is, how treacherous. A spoon stirs coffee. A truck passes loaded with oranges. On one page of the paper, a minister promises history will be repaired; on another, a mother holds a photograph until it becomes a second face. The city has learned to place the cup beside the coffin, to sweep glass from the doorstep and then invite the neighbor in, to kiss the living with lips that still remember the dead.

There are flowers today in a cracked jar. There is dust on the flowers. There are boys kicking a ball against a wall pocked by bullets, arguing over goals with the solemnity of judges. Above them, the sky is impossibly blue, innocent in the way only the sky can be innocent.

And Beirut, calm Beirut, pours tea, folds the newspaper, counts its martyrs, and goes on breathing—half prayer, half wound, half morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of Mahmoud Darwish, beginning with the idea that “no dead on the streets today is a calm day,” set in Beirut after violence.
counterfactuals.output:
No dead on the streets today is a calm day.  
So the city says, rinsing its face  
with a little sea and a little ash.

Beirut gathers her shattered glass  
like a mother gathering lentils from the floor,  
counting what can be cooked,  
what can be named,  
what must be left to the ants of history.

On Hamra, the chairs return to their tables.  
A waiter polishes a cup  
as if polishing the moon’s last witness.  
The coffee is bitter, yes,  
but bitterness is an old citizen here,  
it knows the alleys,  
it pays rent in memory.

No dead on the streets today—  
so the pigeons descend  
with the caution of diplomats.  
The balconies lean out,  
wounded but curious,  
wearing laundry like small flags  
of surrender to the ordinary.

And the sea,  
the sea does not apologize.  
It repeats its blue sentence  
against the stones,  
as if saying: I was here before the noise,  
I will be here after the names  
are carved into silence.

Who will believe us  
when we say we loved life  
between two explosions?  
That we saved the jasmine  
from the dust,  
that a child drew a sun  
on the wall of a shelter,  
and the sun, ashamed, rose?

Beirut,  
you bread of fire,  
you bride with smoke in her hair,  
teach us again  
how to enter morning  
without asking permission from grief.

For today there are no dead in the street,  
only the living,  
walking carefully  
around the invisible bodies  
of yesterday.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal, politically charged free-verse poem about pedestrians, buses, yesterday’s dead, and a woman in a white nightgown saying good morning.
counterfactuals.output:
At the corner, pedestrians bloom  
from the cracked asphalt—  
shoes full of rainwater,  
mouths full of polling stations.

The buses arrive like tired governments,  
belching heat and old promises,  
their windows crowded with faces  
that have forgotten which stop is mercy.

Yesterday’s dead stand in line  
for transfers.

They keep exact change  
in the pockets of their burial clothes.  
They read the headlines backward.  
They nod when the loudspeaker coughs  
and calls them essential.

A flag hangs over the intersection,  
wrinkled as a hospital sheet.  
The traffic lights argue all morning—  
red for obedience,  
green for hunger,  
yellow for the brief philosophy of fear.

And then she appears:

a woman in a white nightgown,  
barefoot on the municipal concrete,  
hair lit like a match  
in the republic of exhaust.

She lifts one hand  
as if blessing the crosswalk,  
as if stopping a tank,  
as if hailing the next impossible bus,

and says,

Good morning.

The phrase opens its small white door.

Inside it:  
bread, sirens, eviction notices,  
the moon with a worker’s badge,  
children drawing suns  
on the backs of court summonses.

The pedestrians pause.  
The buses kneel.  
Yesterday’s dead turn their heads  
toward the sound  
as though called by their true names.

Good morning, she says again,

and all the city’s locked machinery  
shudders—  
not because it believes in dawn,  
but because for one astonished second  
even power remembers  
it was invented by the living.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an English translation-like poem about the aftermath of conflict in Lebanon, mixing daily routine with images of comrades, martyrs, dreams, and the dead resting on pavement.
counterfactuals.output:
After the shelling, we returned to the small things:  
bread in a plastic bag,  
tea darkening in the glass,  
the broom pushing dust from one room to another.

Someone said the street had opened its eyes again.  
Someone said the sea was still there,  
blue as a promise nobody trusted.

My comrades came to me in the morning—  
not all of them living,  
not all of them whole—  
their names folded into my pocket  
like receipts from a shop that no longer stands.

O mother, we have learned the weight of doors,  
how they hang after the blast,  
how they remember the hands that closed them.  
We have learned to sleep in our clothes,  
to count children by their breathing,  
to wake before the planes.

In the square, the martyrs were quiet.  
No speeches rose from their mouths,  
no flags, no songs—  
only the sunlight touching their faces  
with the patience of an old nurse.

And the dead rested on the pavement,  
as if waiting for the bus,  
as if the day were ordinary  
and they had only grown tired  
on the way home.

By noon, the baker opened his oven.  
By noon, a woman washed a shirt in a bucket.  
By noon, the radio named the fallen  
and mispronounced half of them.

Lebanon, small lamp in the wind,  
we dreamed of you while standing in line for water.  
We dreamed of balconies repaired,  
of jasmine returning to the railings,  
of keys fitting locks,  
of fathers not vanishing at checkpoints,  
of sons growing older than their photographs.

At night, the comrades gathered again  
at the edge of sleep.  
They did not accuse us.  
They did not forgive us.  
They simply sat down beside our beds  
and listened  
to the city breathing through its wounds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense lyrical paragraph-poem where a calm day in Beirut feels haunted by death, memory, revolution, and a neighbor’s ordinary morning greeting.
counterfactuals.output: In Beirut the morning arrives deceptively gentle, blue rinsed over the balconies, laundry lifting like small flags of surrender, the sea breathing its salt through the broken mouths of streets, and from the stairwell my neighbor says, as always, sabah el-kheir, with bread under his arm and sleep still in his eyes, as if the day were not standing beside us with ash in its pockets; as if the walls had not learned the names of the dead by heart; as if every bougainvillea did not bloom from a wound. The city pretends to wake, but memory is already awake, seated at the table before the coffee, counting explosions, candles, slogans, mothers, martyrs, the square where we once believed our voices could unbolt the future. Even the pigeons circle like unanswered prayers above the port, above the cranes and ghosts, above the dust that keeps entering our lungs disguised as sunlight. And still my neighbor smiles, ordinary as a spoon, miraculous as water, and I answer him, good morning, though the morning is full of funerals, though beneath our feet the revolution murmurs in its sleep, though every calm thing in Beirut carries, folded inside it, the shape of something shattered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
